111:- **Contribution:** Adapts a small standalone AR LM into a target-independent parallel drafter that predicts K future tokens in one pass using a shared mask token (extrapolates to K_infer > K_train). Conditional Drop-token (COD) training keeps geometrically fewer positions at deeper prediction depths while preserving prefix KV integrity, cutting adaptation cost ~3x.
152:- **Limitation:** Scope (experiments): speedup shrinks with concurrency (Qwen3-4B Math500 4.8x at c=1 to 2.9x at c=32) and the paper notes large blocks raise verification cost when compute-bound, leaving adaptive block-size scheduling to future work. Base drafter degrades beyond its 4K training context without long-context fine-tuning.
162:- **Limitation:** Scope (experiments): gains over EAGLE-3 are modest (1.0-1.36x) and shrink at concurrency 4 for large/MoE targets as verification dominates; evaluated only up to C=4, K≤7, chain drafting on one H200. No intra-block dependency modeling; acceptance only matches AR EAGLE-3.
171:- **Contribution:** Confidence-Adaptive Token (CAT) loss weights each future-token CE+KD term by the cumulative product of target confidences along the ground-truth prefix, a proxy for the probability that position is reached in verification. Stochastic gating of fused target hidden features lets one standalone PARD-style drafter run in target-dependent or target-independent mode.
182:- **Limitation:** Paper-stated: targets inference rather than training cost, implementation mainly adapted to SGLang, and speedup varies across hardware. Scope: Qwen3-4B/8B only, concurrency ≤32, and headline tables compare against public DFlash checkpoints trained on different data.
235:- *Note:* Own acceptance-by-position (Fig. 2, γ=7, values read from plot): Math DFlash .885→.83→.82-.84, EAGLE-3 .81→.85, DSpark .905→.88 (text claims .93 start); Code DFlash .865→.815→.78, EAGLE-3 .77→.785, DSpark .886→.851; Chat DFlash .717→.648→.687, EAGLE-3 .533→.733, DSpark .735→.761. Fig. 4: DFlash τ saturates from draft length 12→16 (math 5.4→5.5) while DSpark keeps rising (6.6→7.2 Markov, ~7.6 RNN). Draft length 16 = anchor + 15 proposals. Max batch: live DeepSeek-V4 traffic up to ~200 concurrent requests/engine (Fig. 8; scheduler shrinks verification budget from ~5-6 to ~3.5 tokens as load rises); latency study at batch 128.
262:- **Limitation:** Paper-stated: only reranks the drafter's top-K, so acceptance is bounded by candidate coverage, and only adjacent slots are coupled. Scope: Qwen3-4B/8B, block 16, concurrency ≤32 on one H100.
272:- **Limitation:** Scope (blog/model card, vendor-run): no paper or disclosed training recipe, and all numbers are Inco AI's own SGLang tests at concurrency ≤32. At concurrency 32 (Qwen3.8-27B, block 8) speedup falls to 1.01-1.45x.
284:- **Contribution:** Each iteration splits a hardware-profiled (roofline) global token budget across requests: it greedily adds the highest draft-path-probability nodes to each request until its expected acceptance meets its TPOT SLO, then fills the rest by global best-first. Candidate-tree depth and width scale with the number of active requests.
330:### ECHO — ECHO: Elastic Speculative Decoding with Sparse Gating for High-Concurrency Scenarios
333:- **Problem:** Static trees waste verification at high concurrency; dynamic trees misjudge and break kernels.
358:- *Note:* ID correct. Concurrent with DDTree (same best-first idea plus a cost-based stop); not compared to DDTree directly. Mean realized trees are ~87-202 nodes at bs=1. Verification is an exact match against the target's own token. Llama-3.1-8B uses a block-10 head; tested on A100/H100/A6000/RTX PRO 6000.
428:- *Note:* ID correct. B=7 uses official DSpark checkpoints; the B=16 drafters were trained by the authors with the DSpark recipe. Concurrent with TreeSpark (same Markov-head idea; TreeSpark cites it). Most cells are single runs. DDTree at N=32 reaches tau 7.49 on the same Qwen3-4B GSM8K setup.
435:- **Limitation:** Own: it needs a drafter with a pretrained causal correction head, and tree verification adds compute, so it targets low-concurrency serving. Fixed large trees degrade under load (B=64 gives 1.06x AR at C=32).
444:- **Contribution:** Packs the top-N path-product prefixes of an unchanged DFlash block into a tree and keeps adding candidates while their mass exceeds a measured verify-time 'token-time exchange rate', so width adapts to GPU/kernel cost without sweeps. Extends the rule to a batch-shared budget via global best-first allocation across requests with a ragged (varlen) Triton tree-verify kernel.
461:- *Note:* ID correct. States that 'the acceptance rate across batch sizes merely fluctuates within a small range' while speedup swings, which matches flat acceptance vs concurrency. Max batch is read from figure axes (~100). The sparsity study edits num_experts_per_token, which changes the target.
467:- **Contribution:** Disaggregates draft and target onto separate tensor-parallel GPU groups that run concurrently. The draft keeps growing a maximum-likelihood token tree, re-rooted after each verification with tree-aware KV reuse, while the target verifies an 8-token subgraph each round; fused GEMM+all-reduce and attention kernels cut small-batch TP latency.
504:*arXiv 2511.13841 · 2025-11 · MLSys 2026 (oral)* · builds on: SuffixDecoding, vanilla SD, RhymeRL, VeRL
527:- **Contribution:** First systematic vLLM study of n-gram, EAGLE/EAGLE-3, draft-model and MTP SD at batch 1-128: target verification dominates step time, and acceptance varies within requests, across requests and across datasets. Oracle simulations quantify the gap to an upper bound that verifies only tokens that will be accepted, plus up to 2.2x more from per-position oracle choice between EAGLE and n-gram.
551:- *Note:* ID correct; ICLR 2026 per arXiv comment. K=2-12 appears only in baseline lookahead sweeps; SD/SSD runs propose 5 tokens, and no tau is reported. Batch-level cache-hit probability is p_hit^b, so misses become near-certain as batch grows and the whole batch stalls; gains are largest at low batch. App. E: with EAGLE-3 the pre-speculating draft conditions on up to 2K self-generated tokens, which lowers acceptance at later positions.
577:- **Contribution:** Scores every draft position in the batch by its prefix-product drafter confidence (estimated survival probability) and verifies only a global top-K, so each request keeps a contiguous high-confidence prefix and low-confidence suffixes are pruned across requests. K is picked from {25,50,75,100}% of B(D+1) by maximizing estimated accepted tokens divided by a startup-profiled step-latency table C(B,rho).
578:- **Limitation:** Stated: per-step variable verify shape does not fit CPU-GPU overlap (Spec-V2) or full CUDA-graph capture, so it runs with piecewise graphs only. Scope: built on DFlash only, greedy draft proposals, concurrency <=64, H20/H800.
581:- *Note:* ID correct. Same Tencent team as AngelSpec, which reuses D-cut. MAT is reported only at conc. 32; there is no MAT-vs-concurrency data (MAT(K) is treated as hardware-independent). input.prompt:
Literature/novelty search (today is 2026-10-08; your knowledge may stop mid-2026, so search the web for newer items). Do NOT write any files. Return a concise structured report as your final message.

Context: someone wants to build a lossless speculative-decoding drafter that conditions on CONCURRENT SIBLING streams (e.g. the other G rollouts of the same prompt in a GRPO group that are being generated at the same time), so acceptance rises with group size. We need prior/concurrent work in the RL-ROLLOUT setting.

Search arXiv (2024 to Oct 2026), OpenReview (incl. ICLR 2027 submissions), MLSys/ASPLOS/OSDI/SOSP/EuroSys/NeurIPS/ICML 2025-26, and GitHub (verl, OpenRLHF, NeMo-RL, slime, AReaL, ROLL, also vLLM/SGLang PRs used by them) for speculative decoding in RL rollouts that drafts from other rollouts. Must cover at least:
- RhymeRL ("History Rhymes", ~2508.18588) - HistoSpec
- SPEC-RL (~2509.23232)
- FastGRPO (~2509.21792)
- Seer: Online Context Learning for Fast Synchronous LLM RL (~2511.14617) - its "grouped speculative decoding"/ Distributed Grouped Draft Server using in-flight responses of the same group. THIS IS KEY: determine exactly whether it uses concurrent in-flight siblings, whether it is model-free (suffix tree) only, acceptance length / speedup numbers, group size.
- DAS (2511.13841), ReSpec (2510.26475), TLT (2511.16665; does its model-free n-gram drafter use sibling rollouts?), NeMo-RL speculative rollouts (2604.26779)
- any 2026 papers: search terms like "group speculative decoding", "rollout group speculative", "sibling rollouts speculative", "intra-group speculative decoding GRPO", "cross-rollout drafting", "speculative rollout reuse", "SpecActor", "rollout reuse speculative", "GRPO speculative decoding 2026", "RL rollout acceleration speculative suffix tree group".
- GitHub: does verl / slime / AReaL / OpenRLHF / NeMo-RL / ROLL ship any sibling/group-aware drafting (e.g., suffix decoding with group sharing, n-gram across group)? Give PR/issue numbers and dates.

For each relevant item give: title, arXiv id + month (or repo/PR + date), venue if any, what it does (model-free vs neural; past/completed rollouts vs concurrent in-flight siblings; same prompt vs different prompts; lossless or lenient), measured acceptance length/speedup, batch/group size evaluated, and closeness to the idea (identical / overlapping / adjacent). VERIFY every arXiv id by opening arxiv.org/abs/<id> (title must match). Mark anything you could not verify. Be concise (aim for <= 900 words).

I couldn't find a 2026 paper that matches your query exactly, meaning a neural drafter that takes the other rollouts in the same GRPO prompt group as conditioning input. Several papers come close, mostly by reusing text across rollouts without a learned drafter.

**Closest matches: reusing text from the same prompt**

- **TLT, "Taming the Long-Tail" (ASPLOS '26):** This one states the idea directly. It says that candidate responses generated for the same prompt often exhibit evident sequence similarity and contain repetitive patterns, such as common mathematical notation or code syntax structures. TLT also supports model-free speculative decoding for early rollout steps, alongside an adaptive drafter that is trained opportunistically on idle resources, counteracting performance dips caused by target model updating.
- **DAS, distribution-aware speculative decoding (Together AI, April 2026):** This is probably the nearest in practice. It uses an adaptive suffix tree drafter, and newly verified tokens are immediately inserted back into the tree, keeping the drafter synchronized with the latest policy at all times. The trees are parallelized per problem, so rollouts for the same problem feed each other's drafts. Together reports up to 50% speedup without touching model outputs.
- **SPEC-RL:** This reuses rollouts across epochs rather than within a group. It treats previous-epoch rollouts as implicit drafts: tokens are verified under the current policy to form a verified prefix, then generation resumes from the first rejection position. The authors report 2–3× lower rollout time.

**A known weakness of drafting from past rollouts**

EfficientRollout (June 2026) argues that history-based drafting methods reuse previous-epoch rollouts as draft proposals and are easy to deploy, but their low-capacity drafters often yield limited block efficiency because past rollouts sparsely cover future trajectories. In its tests, the history-based baseline reuses only 4.4–50.2% of response tokens while adding 10.7–19.5 s of verification overhead. Its own approach is a quantized copy of the target model used as the drafter.

**Related work on learned drafters in group-based RL**

- FastGRPO focuses on concurrency-aware scheduling and online draft learning under high-concurrency group sampling.
- ReSpec studies adaptive draft configurations and reward-weighted drafter adaptation.
- NVIDIA's NeMo-RL integration trains an EAGLE-3 drafter online by reusing rollouts generated by the current policy as supervision. They found that online updating provides limited additional gains when the draft is already well initialized.

These learned drafters are trained on rollouts, but none of them reads sibling rollouts as input when drafting.

**Bottom line:** TLT and DAS have the core insight that same-prompt rollouts overlap heavily. Both use lookup-based drafting rather than a learned drafter that conditions on sibling rollouts. A learned drafter that attends to sibling rollouts in the same group would seem to be an open gap, as far as this search shows.

I couldn't find any paper or system where a draft model uses "cross-sample" or "cross-request" attention, meaning the drafter attends to hidden states from other requests in the same batch to make better guesses. "Cross-attention" does come up, but it means something else. The "batch" papers are about scheduling and compute budgets. The closest real example of requests sharing information is cache-based drafting with no neural attention at all. Here's what the searches turned up:

**1. Cross-attention inside one request (not across requests)**
- **Beagle (Cross-Attention Speculative Decoding, arXiv 2505.24544):** The authors call it "the first, to our knowledge, cross-attention-based Transformer decoder SD model that achieves performance on par with leading self-attention SD models (EAGLE-v2)". Here cross-attention links the draft to the target model's internal states for the same request, not to other requests. The paper also says it focuses on single-batch greedy decoding, and throughput optimization is left for future work.
- It compares against Clover 2, reportedly the most efficient cross-attention-based model, which also works within one request.

**2. Coordinating requests in a batch without sharing representations**
- **TETRIS (ACL 2025):** Picks draft tokens at the batch level, optimizing GPU resource utilization across multiple requests. The authors argue a larger batch gives TETRIS more combinations to choose from. This is coupling across requests, but only through how the shared budget is split.
- **AgentSpec (2026):** Uses Redundancy-aware Budget Allocation, which spreads the draft-token budget across requests based on each one's acceptance probability.
- **EXSpec ("Batch Speculative Decoding Done Right"):** Uses cross-batch scheduling to group sequences of the same length, cutting alignment overhead. "Cross-batch" here is about scheduling, not about information flowing between requests.
- **MineDraft:** Keeps two batches of requests and drafts one while verifying the other.

**3. Batched drafters that are coupled by accident**

**Title:** AgentSpec: Speculative Decoding for Batch Inference of LLM Agents (arXiv:2608.24004, cs.CL; EMNLP 2026)

**Authors:** Xin Wang, Ziming Miao, Yi Zhu, Hui Shen, Zhongwei Wan, Fan Yang, Mi Zhang

**Submitted:** 25 Aug 2026 (v1, 02:49:29 UTC)

**Abstract:** I can't reproduce the full abstract verbatim because of the quote-length limit. Here is a summary:
- LLM agent applications tend to respond slowly. Speculative decoding can speed up inference without lowering output quality, but leading methods slow down considerably at large batch sizes.
- The authors analyze the problem and find two main causes: a "high rejection rate of speculative tokens" and poor use of dynamic token budgets.
- AgentSpec addresses these with two techniques:
  - **Structure-isolated drafting** limits speculation to "semantically coherent segments of the agent workflow." This cuts irrelevant drafts and yields very few rejections.
  - **Redundancy-aware budget allocation** uses agent-level information to make better use of token budget that frees up during inference.
- It was built in vLLM and tested on five workloads and four models from four LLM families. The authors report it outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

**Cross-request drafting?** The page doesn't say. "Redundancy" appears only in the budget-allocation component, described as using "agent-level information." Nothing indicates that drafts are taken from other concurrent requests in the batch.

**Model-free or neural?** Not stated. The abstract doesn't say whether drafting uses a draft model or a model-free approach such as n-gram or retrieval. You would need the full paper to answer this.

content.content:
**Title:** "EfficientRollout: System-Aware Self-Speculative Decoding for RL Rollouts" (arXiv:2606.18967, cs.LG)

**Submission date:** v1 was submitted on 17 June 2026. The current version, v2, was revised on 30 September 2026. The paper was accepted to NeurIPS 2026.

**Abstract:** I can't reproduce the full abstract word-for-word because of the quote-length limit, but here is a close summary:

- **Problem:** RL post-training of LLMs is slowed by rollout generation. Sequential autoregressive sampling and a few very long outputs often determine how long a batch takes to finish.
- **Why standard speculative decoding falls short:** It works well for serving fixed models, but two things differ in RL rollouts:
  - A fixed drafter drifts further from the policy as the policy keeps changing.
  - Active batch sizes shrink during decoding, moving the workload from compute-bound to memory-bound. Parallel verification only helps in the memory-bound phase.
- **Method:** The drafter is "a quantized drafter from the target model." This keeps it tied to the evolving policy without separate pretraining or online adaptation. A system-aware toggle turns speculation on only when it helps. Draft length also adapts to the observed acceptance rate.
- **Results:** Compared with an accelerated autoregressive baseline, rollout latency drops by up to 24.2% and end-to-end latency by up to 15.6%, with no loss in final model quality.

**Drafting from sibling rollouts:** Nothing on this page suggests that. The drafts come from a quantized copy of the target model itself (self-speculative decoding). The abstract never mentions reusing other rollouts in the same group as a draft source.

**Closest match to "group" + speculative decoding (but it isn't about rollouts)**
- **Group Tree Optimization (GTO), ICLR 2026:** This paper borrows GRPO's grouping idea, but to train the small "draft" model, not to speed up rollouts. For a fixed prefix the draft tree is effectively deterministic given the policy, which limits the utility of multiple rollouts from the same state; so to enable variance reduction, they form groups from nearby positions in the same sequence. Code: github.com/hsj576/GTO.

**Speculative decoding for RL/GRPO rollouts**
- **FastGRPO (Sept 2025):** GRPO's slow training is mainly due to generating multiple responses per query, and applying speculative decoding directly gives limited speedup under high-concurrency training. The authors propose a concurrency-aware framework that dynamically adjusts the drafting and verification strategy, plus online training of the draft model. Their setup samples 8 responses for each prompt.
- **DAS, Together AI (April 2026):** This is probably the closest to drafting from other rollouts. It uses a training-free drafter built from recent rollouts, so it adapts to the changing policy without gradient updates. It builds a suffix tree from a sliding window of recent trajectories. Reported result: up to 50% faster with zero degradation in reward quality.
- **NVIDIA NeMo-RL (April 2026):** Speculative decoding implemented in NeMo-RL with a vLLM backend, supporting both synchronous and asynchronous pipelines. At draft length k=3, RL-Zero gets a 1.77× speedup and RL-Think 1.53×. One caution: n-gram drafting is slower than the baseline in both settings (0.7× and 0.5×), even though some drafted tokens are accepted.
- **EfficientRollout (June 2026):** It builds a quantized drafter from the target model itself, so the drafter stays matched to the evolving policy. It cuts rollout and end-to-end latency by up to 19.6% and 12.7%.
- **SpecRL (FAISys '25):** Up to a 2.5× reduction in generation time compared to conventional RL. Its figures also show a group of samples being used when training the draft model with RL.
- **Also relevant:** "Taming the long-tail: efficient reasoning RL training with adaptive drafter" (Hu et al., ASPLOS 2026), cited in the EfficientRollout paper.

If you mean drafting each rollout from the other responses to the same prompt in a GRPO group, DAS and the suffix-tree / n-gram approaches are the closest I found. I didn't find a paper built specifically around that idea. I can search with other wording, such as "cross-rollout," "sibling responses," or "prefix sharing," if that would help.

Papers under double-blind review may not show up in searches, so you'd need to search OpenReview directly to be sure. Here is the closest related work I found:

**Closest to the "sibling" idea (drafting from text the model already generated)**
- **DAS (Together AI):** It builds its drafter from recent rollouts, so it can continuously adapt to the changing policy without any gradient updates. Newly checked tokens are immediately inserted back into the tree, keeping the drafter synchronized with the latest policy. The design targets the prompt reuse unique to RL, and the authors report cutting compute costs by up to 50% with no degradation in model quality.
- **SPEC-RL:** It reuses prior trajectory segments as speculative prefixes and extends them via a draft-and-verify mechanism, cutting rollout time by 2–3× without compromising policy quality. Note that it reuses rollouts from earlier epochs, not siblings in the same group.

**Learned or model-derived drafters for GRPO-style RL**
- **FastGRPO (arXiv 2509.21792):** It adjusts drafting and verification according to real-time concurrency levels and adds online draft learning so the drafter keeps adapting to the changing target model. It reports end-to-end speedups of 2.35x to 2.72x.
- **ReSpec (arXiv 2510.26475):** It points out that methods like GRPO and DAPO generate multiple candidate completions per prompt and compute updates from relative comparisons inside each group. Its fixes are dynamically tuning SD configurations, evolving the drafter via knowledge distillation, and weighting updates by rollout rewards, reaching up to 4.5× speedup.
- **EfficientRollout (ICML 2026):** It induces a quantized drafter directly from the target model, keeping it coupled to the evolving policy without separate drafter training. It also argues that drafting from rollout history tends to accept few tokens per step, because past rollouts sparsely cover future trajectories.

The specific idea you're asking about, where agents fanned out from the same context use each other's outputs as draft tokens, already exists in the research literature. I didn't find it as a named feature in a production serving system. Here are the most relevant results, grouped by topic.

## 1. Drafts taken from sibling outputs (closest match)

**Speculative Decoding for Multi-Sample Inference (arXiv 2503.05330)** comes closest. It targets multi-sample reasoning scenarios, such as self-consistency and Best-of-N sampling. How it works:
- It leverag[es] the overlapping token subsequences generated across parallel reasoning paths to build a dynamic draft token pool.
- At each inference step, the most recent tokens from any path are used as queries to retrieve matching prefixes from other paths via suffix-based matching.
- Candidate drafts are then organized into a weighted directed acyclic graph (DAG), where the edge weights reflect transition probabilities derived from the LLM's distribution. It needs no auxiliary model or external database.
- Caveats: the method is not combined with speculative decoding methods optimized for batch processing, so its acceleration effect on time requires further exploration. Also, the probabilistic aggregation mechanism incurs non-negligible overhead when processing a large number of parallel paths.

## 2. Retrieval-based drafting in multi-agent pipelines

**AgSpec (arXiv 2610.01108, Oct 2026)**:
- AgSpec retrieves from session, workspace, and global corpora, retaining the ongoing session trajectory and indexing opened files in the agent's emission format.
- It bounds each agent's draft length with an offline-profiled cap and adapts the length online from verification feedback.
- Results: on two repository-level multi-agent coding benchmarks, AgSpec outperforms five retrieval-based drafters and EAGLE-3 in most evaluated settings, raising generation throughput over autoregressive decoding up to 4.37× at batch size 1 and 4.76× at batch size 16.
- Design note relevant to your idea: the authors keep corpora separate per user, because folding every workspace into a global corpus shared by all users would be difficult to manage.

## 3. Sharing the context itself (the KV-cache side)

A Zylos Research overview (May 2026) lists multi-agent orchestration where all sub-agents share the same system context as a main use case for prefix caching. It adds that the RelayCaching paper (2025) demonstrated over 80% KV cache reuse across agent collaborations, reducing TTFT by up to 4.7× with negligible accuracy degradation. In its description of a typical stack, shared contexts are handled with radix-tree prefix caching.

## 4. Practical limits of batch inference

- **Speedups shrink as batches grow.** EAGLE-3 provides 1.81× throughput improvement at batch size 2 and maintains 1.38× at batch size 64, because the decode step becomes more compute-efficient with batching, reducing the relative benefit of speculation.
- **Ragged batches.** Sequences in a batch accept different numbers of draft tokens, which break[s] right-alignment and corrupt[s] position IDs, attention masks, and KV-cache state. The EQSPEC/EXSPEC paper fixes this with cross-batch scheduling that dynamically groups same-length sequences. It also notes that neither vLLM nor SGLang currently supports continuous batching speculative decoding with external draft models.
- **Overlapped drafting fails more often in big batches.** With SSD, if any request's predicted bonus token is wrong, the whole batch loses its precomputed continuation and reverts to serial drafting. MineDraft (2603.18016) runs drafting and verification in parallel enabling overlapped execution across two alternating batches.

## Takeaways
- For sibling agents with a shared prefix, the most direct approach is suffix-match retrieval over the siblings' in-progress outputs, as in the multi-sample paper and AgSpec, combined with prefix caching for the shared context.
- No source I found evaluates sibling drafting at large batch sizes under continuous batching. That combination looks like an open gap.
- One more lead from my own knowledge, not these search results: SuffixDecoding, a model-free drafter built on suffix trees over prior outputs aimed at agentic workloads, is worth looking up.

I couldn't find a paper that does exactly this: a trained neural drafter that drafts tokens for one sample by reading the hidden states of the other samples running in parallel for self-consistency. The closest work is training-free. Separately, there are many 2026 neural drafters, but they only look at the hidden states of the main (target) model for a single sequence.

**Closest match: consensus drafting with no trained drafter (Li et al., March 2025)**
- "Speculative Decoding for Multi-Sample Inference" (arXiv 2503.05330) is built for multi-sample reasoning scenarios, such as self-consistency and Best-of-N sampling. It exploits the intrinsic consensus of parallel generation paths to synthesize high-quality draft tokens without requiring auxiliary models or external databases.
- The idea behind it: when a model generates several answers in parallel, these outputs share common substeps—such as intermediate equations in math problems—while differing in ordering or phrasing. And because all paths stem from the same model, their substeps naturally mirror its output tendencies, unlike externally sourced drafts.
- How it works: it aggregat[es] via probabilistic DAG construction and verif[ies] only high-scoring consensus tokens.
- More samples help: accept length increases as the sampling size grows.
- Its stated limits: it is not combined with speculative decoding methods optimized for batch processing, so its acceleration effect on time requires further exploration, and the probabilistic aggregation mechanism incurs non-negligible overhead when processing a large number of parallel paths.
- Survey pages still list this as the main "consensus-driven" approach. One describes self-speculative methods that extend to multi-sample reasoning by leveraging cross-sample consensus structures.

**Related 2026 neural drafters (hidden states of the main model, one sample only)**
- **DFlash, DSpark, EAGLE-3:** EAGLE-3 drafts autoregressively from target-model hidden states, DFlash drafts parallel blocks from target-model hidden states, and DSpark adds lightweight causal correction and confidence-based prefix selection.
- **Make Every Draft Count (Feb 2026):** it predicts at the hidden states level and postpone[s] the integrating token information after the hidden states generation, so the draft hidden states are not contaminated by incorrect tokens, enabling hidden state reuse. It reports up to a 3.3x speedup against standard speculative decoding.
- **H-Spec (Sept 2026):** a hybrid Mamba-attention parallel drafter that reuses the main model's KV cache directly instead of keeping a separate drafter-side cache.
- **DPara (Sept 2026):** a PSD framework that reuses effective parallel drafters yet guarantees backbone--verification overlap in every round.
- **EDR (2026):** a training objective that consistently improves mean accepted length over the original drafters and existing training objectives for DSpark and DFly.

**Gap**
None of these results trains a drafter to look across sibling samples' hidden states, for example via cross-attention over the other self-consistency paths. That combination looks open, or at least I couldn't find it in what I searched. Two things suggest it could pay off: Li et al. show more samples give longer accepted drafts, and the new drafters already work on hidden states. One open question is batching cost. Li et al. found that a known batched method (BASS on EAGLE-2), when the batch size is greater than or equals to 8, it even becomes slower than vanilla decoding.

I couldn't find a paper that does exactly this: a trained neural drafter that drafts tokens for one sample by reading the hidden states of the other samples running in parallel for self-consistency. The closest work is training-free. Separately, there are many 2026 neural drafters, but they only look at the hidden states of the main (target) model for a single sequence.

**Closest match: consensus drafting with no trained drafter (Li et al., March 2025)**
- "Speculative Decoding for Multi-Sample Inference" (arXiv 2503.05330) is built for multi-sample reasoning scenarios, such as self-consistency and Best-of-N sampling. It exploits the intrinsic consensus of parallel generation paths to synthesize high-quality draft tokens without requiring auxiliary models or external databases.
- The idea behind it: when a model generates several answers in parallel, these outputs share common substeps—such as intermediate equations in math problems—while differing in ordering or phrasing. And because all paths stem from the same model, their substeps naturally mirror its output tendencies, unlike externally sourced drafts.
- How it works: it aggregat[es] via probabilistic DAG construction and verif[ies] only high-scoring consensus tokens.
- More samples help: accept length increases as the sampling size grows.
- Its stated limits: it is not combined with speculative decoding methods optimized for batch processing, so its acceleration effect on time requires further exploration, and the probabilistic aggregation mechanism incurs non-negligible overhead when processing a large number of parallel paths.
- Survey pages still list this as the main "consensus-driven" approach. One describes self-speculative methods that extend to multi-sample reasoning by leveraging cross-sample consensus structures.

**Related 2026 neural drafters (hidden states of the main model, one sample only)**
- **DFlash, DSpark, EAGLE-3:** EAGLE-3 drafts autoregressively from target-model hidden states, DFlash drafts parallel blocks from target-model hidden states, and DSpark adds lightweight causal correction and confidence-based prefix selection.
- **Make Every Draft Count (Feb 2026):** it predicts at the hidden states level and postpone[s] the integrating token information after the hidden states generation, so the draft hidden states are not contaminated by incorrect tokens, enabling hidden state reuse. It reports up to a 3.3x speedup against standard speculative decoding.
- **H-Spec (Sept 2026):** a hybrid Mamba-attention parallel drafter that reuses the main model's KV cache directly instead of keeping a separate drafter-side cache.
- **DPara (Sept 2026):** a PSD framework that reuses effective parallel drafters yet guarantees backbone--verification overlap in every round.
- **EDR (2026):** a training objective that consistently improves mean accepted length over the original drafters and existing training objectives for DSpark and DFly.

**Gap**
None of these results trains a drafter to look across sibling samples' hidden states, for example via cross-attention over the other self-consistency paths. That combination looks open, or at least I couldn't find it in what I searched. Two things suggest it could pay off: Li et al. show more samples give longer accepted drafts, and the new drafters already work on hidden states. One open question is batching cost. Li et al. found that a known batched method (BASS on EAGLE-2), when the batch size is greater than or equals to 8, it even becomes slower than vanilla decoding.

Your query matches **"Seer: Online Context Learning for Fast Synchronous LLM Reinforcement Learning"** (arXiv 2511.14617), a paper from Moonshot AI researchers.

**Main idea**
Seer starts from one observation: requests sharing the same prompt exhibit strong similarities in output lengths and response patterns. RL algorithms like GRPO generate G (typically 8–16) responses per prompt, so these similar groups appear constantly during training. Seer uses this in three coordinated techniques: (1) divided rollout for dynamic load balancing, (2) context-aware scheduling to mitigate long-tail request delays, and (3) adaptive grouped speculative decoding to accelerate generation.

**Distributed Grouped Draft Server (DGDS)**
- **How it drafts:** Seer deploys a Distributed Grouped Draft Server (DGDS) that maintains a Compressed Suffix Tree (CST) for each group, aggregating token sequences from all requests within the same group. This yields a highly accurate, dynamic "draft model" that is inherently synchronized with the target model.
- **Why not a normal draft model:** Conventional SD methods struggle to simultaneously achieve high draft accuracy and low draft overhead in RL settings, where both the request workload and the target model itself evolve dynamically.
- **Sharing across machines:** Inference instances asynchronously share newly generated tokens with DGDS, which aggregates these across all requests in a group.
- **Deployment:** It supports multi-server deployment mode, with clients automatically routing to appropriate servers via request group hashing. The draft client deploys as an embedded library within the same process as the inference engine, providing zero-copy batch interfaces to minimize speculation overhead.
- **Adaptive drafting:** DGDS uses a Marginal-Benefit-Aware Adaptive Speculation policy that balances overall throughput with the latency of high-priority requests. During low-concurrency periods (the long-tail phase), larger draft lengths are permitted to preferentially accelerate remaining requests.

**Speculative decoding results**
- Compared to vanilla CST-based SD without group context, it increases the mean acceptance length by 0.22.
- In the later stage of rollout, speculative decoding with full grouped pattern references can improve the number of accepted draft tokens by up to 119% compared to a baseline that only uses per-request history.
- Ablation, compared with no speculative decoding: Adaptive grouped speculative decoding brought 30% end-to-end throughput improvement · Without group context sharing, improvement dropped to 19% Without adaptive strategy, improvement was only 3%.

**Overall results**
- Evaluated on 256 H800 GPUs across multiple production-grade RL workloads, using Moonlight, Qwen2-VL-72B, and Kimi-K2.
- Seer improves rollout throughput by 74 percent to 97 percent across these workloads relative to veRL with the same RL algorithm and vLLM based inference engine. Tail latency is reduced by 75 percent to 93 percent.
- Contribution of each part: Divided Rollout as the foundation brought 27%-35% performance improvement through dynamic load balancing · Context-Aware Scheduling utilizing length information further improved performance by 6%-13% Adaptive Grouped Speculative Decoding contributed the largest single-component improvement at 30%-44%.

**Criticism**
One automated review on Pith says the evaluation is thin. It notes that the absence of quantified support for the core assumption and baseline details reduces the immediate strength of the contribution.

The full paper is at arxiv.org/abs/2511.14617 (latest version v3).

I couldn't find a paper that does exactly this: speeding up MCTS or tree search for LLM reasoning by using a sibling node's already-generated continuation as the draft for speculative decoding. The two searches did turn up several closely related lines of work, which together suggest the idea could work and may not be well covered yet.

**1. Reusing text from other rollouts as drafts (the closest match)**
- **TLAR (Trajectory-Retrieval Speculative Decoding)** asks when a model's own past output makes useful drafts. It supplies an additional candidate source to this draft–verify architecture: continuations already present in the generated trajectory. The authors also compare current history with control sources and another rollout of the same problem. That comparison is the nearest thing to sibling reuse. One finding matters for your idea: "The same problem need not provide the same drafts." Retrieval costs something too, because every retrieved candidate must be verified by the target model which adds computation, while reusable content does not appear at every position in a reasoning trace.
- **Graft (Hybrid Tree Construction)** combines a multi-token-prediction drafter with an n-gram branch that dynamically aggregates group generation history and can retrieve long high quality continuations when rollout trajectories share reasoning templates, tool use patterns, or local solution structures. It targets agentic reinforcement learning, where it can exploit the strong local repetition created by grouped rollouts.
- **EfficientRollout** is a warning sign. In its experiments, a baseline that drafts from earlier rollouts does not reduce rollout-generation latency. Even after rollout history becomes available, it reuses only 4.4–50.2% of response tokens while adding 10.7–19.5 s of verification overhead.
- **Earlier retrieval methods** that TLAR cites: SuffixDecoding uses suffix-tree statistics (Oliaro et al., 2026), SAM-Decoding uses suffix automata (Hu et al., 2025), Token Recycling reuses candidate transitions (Luo et al., 2025), and STAND uses stochastic n-gram statistics from reasoning trajectories (Song et al., 2025).

**2. SuffixDecoding, a ready-made mechanism**
In SuffixDecoding, two suffix trees track ongoing inference (top-left) and previous outputs (bottom-left). It constructs a speculation tree (middle) by selecting the most likely continuations, scoring them based on frequency statistics. The authors say the motivation is that reasoning loops [Wang et al., 2023a, Madaan et al., 2023] regenerate similar token sequences. vLLM already supports it as a speculative method. In vLLM's own assessment, though, simpler methods such as n-gram and suffix decoding provide modest speedups. In practice, an MCTS engine could add each node's rollouts to a suffix cache scoped to that search tree, which would give you sibling reuse with little extra work.

**3. MCTS for reasoning that keeps its rollouts**
- One MCTS-for-reasoning implementation stores everything it generates during rollouts. Here, we add every rollout node to the tree. This preserves the full reasoning trace and allows reuse of reasoning steps in future simulations. It's more expensive per simulation, but reasoning steps are expensive to generate anyway, so you want to keep them. It reuses whole reasoning steps rather than using them as speculative drafts.
- The TreeCoder framework notes that even when MCTS stays at the root, their rolled-out sequences are still stored within the tree. That stored text is exactly what a drafter could pull from.

**4. Recycling rejected branches inside speculative decoding**
- **Carryover Drafting** points out that conventional drafters retain only the representations of accepted tokens, leaving the substantial verifier computation spent on rejected tokens effectively wasted. It found that these discarded hidden states generated during target forward retain useful information about future tokens that can improve subsequent drafts.
- **Lyanna** works along the same lines. Upon verification completion, Lyanna identifies reusable hidden states and re-samples new drafts from them.

**Takeaways**
Reusing sibling continuations as drafts sits between suffix/retrieval drafting and tree search that keeps its rollouts, and I found nothing that ties the two together in an MCTS setting. The evidence above points to two things to watch:
- **Low overlap:** acceptance depends on how much sibling branches actually share. Two rollouts of the same problem don't reliably produce matching drafts, and history-based drafting reused only part of the response tokens in RL.
- **Extra verification cost:** every retrieved draft has to be checked by the target model, so you probably need a rule that decides when to try retrieval. TLAR's approach, based on acceptance at earlier positions, is a good place to start.

You may also want to search specifically for "speculative" variants of MCTS or beam search for reasoning, which these searches didn't cover.

**Title:** "Trajectory-Retrieval Speculative Decoding: When Does a Model's Own History Help?" (arXiv:2610.07350, cs.AI, 33 pages, CC0 license)

**Authors:** Yuyang Dai and Yushun Dong. The submission history lists the submitter as "Yuyang Tsai," which doesn't match the author list.

**Date:** Submitted Monday, 5 Oct 2026 (v1).

**Abstract (paraphrased, with short quotes):**
- Long chain-of-thought reasoning makes sequential decoding expensive. It also builds up a history of continuations that might be reused.
- The authors study when that history yields useful drafts and how it complements an existing drafter.
- "Controlled source comparisons reveal trajectory-specific reuse." This finding motivates their method, Trajectory-Local Adaptive Retrieval (TLAR).
- TLAR pulls approximately matched continuations from the current trajectory. It uses recent verification results to decide when retrieval activates and how many candidates to consider.
- Retrieved and model-generated drafts share one candidate tree. Exact verification preserves the target model's output distribution.
- Evaluation covers code debugging, math, and open-ended writing.
- Pairing TLAR with strong retrieval baselines "improves token acceptance under matched verification budgets." It also raises end-to-end throughput relative to the draft-model baseline.

**Sibling rollout vs. own history:** The page doesn't say directly. "Controlled source comparisons" that found "trajectory-specific reuse" suggests the authors compared different retrieval sources and found the current trajectory works best. Whether sibling samples of the same problem were one of those sources isn't stated.

**Acceptance / speedup numbers:** None are given. The abstract only reports qualitative gains in acceptance and throughput.

**Concurrent vs. completed siblings:** Not mentioned.

**Model-free or neural drafter:** It's a hybrid. TLAR's drafting is retrieval-based, so it needs no neural model. It is combined with drafts from a separate draft model in the shared tree, and it is benchmarked against a "draft-model baseline."

The full PDF or HTML version would be needed to confirm the sibling comparison details and the actual numbers.

**Authors:** Yuyang Dai and Yushun Dong. The submission history lists the submitter as "Yuyang Tsai," which doesn't match the author list.

**Date:** Submitted Monday, 5 Oct 2026 (v1).

**Abstract (paraphrased, with short quotes):**
- Long chain-of-thought reasoning makes sequential decoding expensive. It also builds up a history of continuations that might be reused.
- The authors study when that history yields useful drafts and how it complements an existing drafter.
- "Controlled source comparisons reveal trajectory-specific reuse." This finding motivates their method, Trajectory-Local Adaptive Retrieval (TLAR).
- TLAR pulls approximately matched continuations from the current trajectory. It uses recent verification results to decide when retrieval activates and how many candidates to consider.
- Retrieved and model-generated drafts share one candidate tree. Exact verification preserves the target model's output distribution.
- Evaluation covers code debugging, math, and open-ended writing.
- Pairing TLAR with strong retrieval baselines "improves token acceptance under matched verification budgets." It also raises end-to-end throughput relative to the draft-model baseline.

**Sibling rollout vs. own history:** The page doesn't say directly. "Controlled source comparisons" that found "trajectory-specific reuse" suggests the authors compared different retrieval sources and found the current trajectory works best. Whether sibling samples of the same problem were one of those sources isn't stated.

**Acceptance / speedup numbers:** None are given. The abstract only reports qualitative gains in acceptance and throughput.

**Concurrent vs. completed siblings:** Not mentioned.

**Model-free or neural drafter:** It's a hybrid. TLAR's drafting is retrieval-based, so it needs no neural model. It is combined with drafts from a separate draft model in the shared tree, and it is benchmarked against a "draft-model baseline."

The full PDF or HTML version would be needed to confirm the sibling comparison details and the actual numbers.

**Paper:** *Draft Less, Retrieve More: Hybrid Tree Construction for Speculative Decoding*. The authors are Yuhao Shen, Tianyu Liu, Xinyi Hu, Quan Kong, Baolin Zhang, Jun Dai, Jun Zhang, Shuang Ge, Lei Chen, Yue Li, Mingcheng Wan and Cong Wang (Zhejiang University, Alibaba's Qwen Applications Business Group, USTC). It is arXiv:2605.20104v1 [cs.LG], dated 19 May 2026.

**The RL rollout idea is only a proposal.** It appears in the "Future Works" section (4.5) as a sketched extension. The paper implements and evaluates nothing for RL.

**How the n-gram branch uses group history:**
- The paper says only that it "dynamically aggregates group generation history." It can retrieve long continuations when rollouts "share reasoning templates, tool use patterns, or local solution structures."
- **Siblings of the same group:** This is implied by the reference to Seer, which mines "local n-gram overlap from responses in the same rollout group." The paper doesn't explicitly say Graft would do the same.
- **In-flight vs. completed rollouts:** The paper doesn't say.

**Relationship to the MTP drafter:**
- The paper describes the two as separate branches merged in one grafted tree. The MTP branch "stabilizes the lower bound while retrieval raises the upper bound."
- Confidence pruning would decide which MTP positions are unreliable, and retrieved candidates would be grafted into those slots.
- Nothing suggests retrieved content would be fed into the MTP drafter as conditioning. This matches the main method, where retrieval only fills tree slots and verification is unchanged.

**Numbers:** The paper gives no acceptance lengths, speedups, batch sizes or group sizes for RL or GRPO. Its reported results come from other settings:
- **Short-context:** up to 5.41× speedup; +21.8% average over EAGLE-3 on Qwen3-235B (2.09× vs 1.71×).
- **Long-context:** 3.22× average on LLaMA3.1-8B (MAT ~6.0–6.4); +16.6% over EAGLE3-64K on Qwen3-14B.
- **Temperature sampling (T=1):** 3.43× on LLaMA3.1-8B and 2.26× on Qwen3-8B.
- **DFlash on Qwen3-8B:** average speedup rises from 3.40× to 3.71×.
- **High-batch serving (SGLang, Qwen3-8B, batch sizes 1–16):** Graft beat EAGLE3 on both throughput and MAT. The exact figures are in Appendix D, which is truncated in the provided content.

Give the numbers (acceptance, hit rate, accepted length) per source, the model, temperature, and the conclusion "the same problem need not provide the same drafts". Also is the sibling rollout a completed sample or concurrent?

toolu_01Q4YCQyVC9jE4upJFU1PVsS.prompt: Find the "controlled source comparison" experiment: which retrieval sources were compared (current trajectory, another rollout/sample of the same problem, other problems, etc.)? Give the numbers (acceptance, hit rate, accepted length) per source, the model, temperature, and the conclusion "the same problem need not provide the same drafts". Also is the sibling rollout a completed sample or concurrent?

content.content:
# Controlled source comparison (Section 3)

**Sources compared.** All sources were scored against the same fixed target trajectory and acceptance rule:
- **Within:** the current generated history.
- **Cross:** "another trajectory from the same target model and dataset," limited to the same available history length. This changes both the problem and the trajectory.
- **Shuffled:** the current history with its blocks reordered.
- **Unigram:** token frequencies, with no context matching.

Within, Cross and Shuffled all use the same matcher (c=4, ε=1, τ=512, d=4).

**Same-prompt follow-up.** This separates the problem from the trajectory. For 24 code-debugging problems, the authors compared own history against a second rollout of the same problem that used a different random seed. Results are shown as mean accepted tokens with 95% bootstrap intervals.

**Models.** Qwen3-8B, Mistral-Small-3.2-24B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, across code (100 tasks), math (24) and open-ended writing (24).

**Metric.** Mean exactly accepted length (E_exact). No hit-rate or acceptance-rate figures per source appear in the visible text.

**Numbers.** These are not in the provided content. The figures appear without values, and the exact values are said to be in Appendix Table 8, which was cut off.

**Temperature.** Not stated in the visible text.

**Results.**
- **Finding 1:** Within beats all three controls for all three models in code and math. In open-ended writing the effect is weaker: Mistral's advantage shrinks, and Qwen "does not exceed Unigram."
- **Finding 2 ("The same problem need not provide the same drafts"):** Qwen and Mistral favor their own history over the sibling rollout. Llama shows the reverse, so its reusable drafts "appear to depend more on the shared problem than on its own rollout."
- **Finding 3:** Successful retrievals cluster, meaning a hit is more likely right after another hit.

**Completed or concurrent sibling?** The text doesn't say explicitly. However, the evaluation is offline replay on fixed, pre-generated trajectories, and Cross is truncated to the same history length. That suggests the sibling was a previously completed sample, cut to a matching prefix, rather than a concurrently generated one. This is an inference, not a stated fact.

content.content:
# Source comparison values (Table 8) and sampling settings

## Table 8: mean exactly accepted tokens (E_exact)

| Task | Model | Within | Cross | Shuffled | Unigram |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Code debugging | Qwen3-8B | 1.2184 | 0.0139 | 0.0161 | 0.0658 |
| Code debugging | Mistral-24B | 2.7266 | 0.0069 | 0.0326 | 0.0585 |
| Code debugging | Llama-3.1-8B | 1.0612 | 0.0046 | 0.0236 | 0.0539 |
| Mathematics | Qwen3-8B | 1.0620 | 0.0037 | 0.0155 | 0.0627 |
| Mathematics | Mistral-24B | 1.1888 | 0.0039 | 0.0268 | 0.0713 |
| Mathematics | Llama-3.1-8B | 2.2378* | 0.0141 | 0.0539 | 0.0761 |
| Open-ended | Qwen3-8B | 0.0274 | 0.0016 | 0.0003 | 0.0535 |
| Open-ended | Mistral-24B | 0.1849 | 0.0003 | 0.0011 | 0.0435 |
| Open-ended | Llama-3.1-8B | 0.3283 | 0.0020 | 0.0121 | 0.0561 |

*This is the cleaned value. It excludes seven repetition-flagged trajectories; before removal the mean was 7.03.

- Unigram is the strongest control in every row.
- The source measurement cap is 32 tokens.
- An older snapshot (Table 9) adds DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B in place of Mistral. Its code, math and open-ended Within values are 0.6599, 0.8183 and 0.1170. Its Within/Unigram lift ranges from 0.5× to 29.4×.

## Same-prompt, different-seed follow-up (Table 12)

This uses 24 paired code-debugging problems per model, with exact context matching on an equal-length prefix.

| Model | Within | Other seed |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-8B | 2.0814 [1.4340, 2.9241] | 1.2653 [0.9282, 1.6487] |
| Mistral-24B | 1.4354 [1.1416, 1.7132] | 0.8614 [0.6644, 1.1190] |
| Llama-3.1-8B | 0.8243 [0.3755, 1.4092] | 1.1134 [0.6498, 1.6673] |

- Mistral's paired difference is 0.5740, with interval [0.1060, 1.0065].
- Llama is the exception: its other-seed rollout scores higher than its own history.

## Sampling settings

- Target generation uses temperature 0.6, top-p = 0.95, and "a maximum of 4,096 new tokens."
- Examples are sorted by identifier and sampled with seed 20260217 before retrieval evaluation. This seed selects the dataset examples; it is not a generation seed.
- The same-prompt comparison uses "two generation seeds" per problem, but the seed values themselves are not given.

    try:
        d=json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(url,timeout=40))
    except Exception as e:
        print("ERR",t,e);continue
    for n in d.get("notes",[]):

        ab=c.get("abstract",{}).get("value","")
        txt=(ti+" "+ab).lower()

        seen.add(n["id"])
        print("###",ti,"|",n["id"],"|",hit)
EOF

content.content:
### RANA: Accelerating Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Speculative Decoding | T0dAyKIH7J | 2026-09-19
The evolution of Large Language Models (LLMs) toward reasoning-intensive agents relies heavily on Reinforcement Learning (RL) for alignment, e.g., RL human feedback (RLHF). However, the RLHF rollout phase suffers from severe computational inefficiencies, particularly in multi-turn interactions where sequential dependencies exacerbate the long-tail effect and lead to GPU underutilization. While recent work has explored speculative decoding (SD) to accelerate RLHF rollouts, they overlook the structural properties of agentic multi-turn interactions, i.e., contextual continuity, entropy decay, and hardware sensitivity, leaving substantial optimization potential unexploited. In this paper, we propose RANA (Rollout Adaptive N-Gram Accelerator), a system that accelerates multi-turn agentic RLHF rollouts by systematically exploiting these structural properties. RANA consists of three innovative components: (1) a Tree-based N-gram Speculative Decoding mechanism that leverages historical context for model-free drafting; (2) a Load-Adaptive Controller that dynamically toggles speculation based on Roofline analysis to avoid compute-bound contention; and (3) an Entropy-aware Scheduler that leverages entropy decay to align low-entropy rollouts with the execution tail, where speculative decoding yields the greatest benefit. Experiments show that RANA achieves up to 3.74x speedup, significantly outperforming prior approaches.

### HIGAP: Bridging the Overhead Gap in History-Based Speculative Rollout for MoE RL | sLpTzI6XxI | 2026-09-18
Rollout generation is a major bottleneck in reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models. History-based speculative rollout can reduce this cost by reusing trajectories from previous training steps as drafts, but its rollout-stage savings do not necessarily translate into end-to-end speedup, especially for mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. Expensive actor verification, redundant old-log-probability computation, and actor drift can substantially offset the benefits of history reuse. We present $\textbf{HiGAP}$, a history-based speculative rollout framework that bridges this overhead gap through full-pipeline optimization.  HiGAP adaptively bounds historical draft lengths to regulate history reuse and verification overhead, leverages verification probabilities to partially bypass old-log-probability recomputation, and mitigates history staleness under actor drift through post-update probability caching and advantage-guided history updates. Across three MoE and one dense models, HiGAP consistently reduces end-to-end step time and improves training throughput while maintaining competitive training effectiveness. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, HiGAP reduces step time by 11.6\% and improves throughput by 12.7\% over vanilla GRPO, while improving the average score by 12.3 points across nine mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

### DLite: History-Free Speculative Decoding for Agentic AI | UwMYxYHQSG | 2026-08-27
Speculative decoding has become a mainstream technique for accelerating large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight draft model to gener- ate candidate tokens that are subsequently verified by the target model. How- ever, agentic workloads introduce long and continuously evolving contexts and frequent multi-turn interactions. Under such workloads, we observe that existing draft models suffer from up to an 80% degradation in acceptance length, while maintaining their historical KV cache introduces substantial system overhead. In this paper, we identify the growing historical context as a common source of both problems and introduce DLite, a history-free speculative decoding framework for agentic AI. DLite directly reuses contextual hidden states from the target model and performs local speculative prediction without explicitly maintaining the his- torical context, transforming an increasingly complex modeling problem into local simple prediction problem. A lightweight sequential head further restores intra- block causal dependencies with low overhead. To effectively train this heteroge- neous history-free architecture, we introduce a tailored two-stage training strat- egy. Experiments on general-purpose, long-context and agentic workloads show that DLite achieves 2∼6 acceptance length and outperforms the state-of-the-art speculative decoding method, DSpark, up to 70%.

### Speculative Multi-Trajectory Decoding for Efficient Multimodal LLM Planning | 3s9Dg3RAwP | 2026-09-19
Multimodal large language model (MLLM) planners typically serialize trajectories into token sequences and decode them autoregressively, making sequential generation a major inference bottleneck that becomes more severe when multiple candidates are required. To address this issue, we propose Speculative Multi-Trajectory Decoding (SMTD), a target-verified framework that accelerates trajectory generation through a unified draft–verify–select process while keeping the pretrained OneVL target model frozen. Lightweight Medusa and anchored-GRU drafters first propose blocks of future trajectory tokens, which are verified in parallel by the target model to reduce sequential evaluations while preserving target-consistent generation. Building on this mechanism, SMTD extends speculative decoding to multi-trajectory planning via speculative multi-sampling, efficiently producing multiple verified candidates. A Unified Online Candidate Selector (UOCS) then scores these candidates and selects the final trajectory at inference time. Experiments on NAVSIM, ROADWork, and Impromptu demonstrate consistent latency reductions with competitive planning quality. On NAVSIM, SMTD reduces mean decoding latency from 5.221 s to 1.349 s. The remaining gap between selected and oracle candidates further identifies online selection as a key bottleneck after generation is accelerated.

### NebulaSD: Many-for-Many Speculative Decoding | 8SZkaiC1UC | 2026-09-17
Speculative decoding accelerates Large Language Model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight draft model to propose candidate tokens for parallel verification by a target model. Drafting and verification, however, exhibit different service characteristics and favor different batch configurations, making fixed draft-target coupling inefficient under concurrent workloads. Existing distributed designs can physically separate the two stages, but often retain request or batch affinities that prevent their capacities from being shared globally. We present NebulaSD, a many-for-many, or M-for-N, speculative decoding system that organizes draft and target workers into independently schedulable resource pools and dynamically reconstructs stage-specific batches from shared request pools. Links: [{"title":"Decoding Speculative Decoding Minghao Yan*, Saurabh Agarwal,","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.01528"},{"title":"Closer Look at Efficient Inference Methods: A Survey of Speculative Decoding","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2411.13157v2"},{"title":"Decoding Speculative Decoding","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2402.01528v4"}]

I couldn't find anything about a method called RANA ("Rollout Adaptive N-Gram Accelerator"). Two searches turned up no paper, blog, or repo with that name. It may be very new, not indexed yet, or listed under another title. If you have an arXiv ID or author names, I can search for those. I did find several closely related papers on speeding up RL rollouts with speculative decoding:

**1. Distribution-Aware Speculative Decoding (DAS), Together AI (April 2026).** This is the closest match to what RANA's name suggests: an adaptive drafter built from past rollouts that needs no training.
- Claims rollouts up to 50% faster, zero degradation in reward quality.
- Uses an adaptive suffix tree drafter that accelerates generation and scales gracefully over long training horizons, plus a length-aware scheduling strategy that reduces rollout stragglers through inter-GPU load balancing and intra-GPU speculation budget allocation.
- Because as the policy evolves throughout RL training, a static drafter quickly becomes stale, it uses a training-free drafter built from recent rollouts, so it can continuously adapt to the changing policy without any gradient updates.
- DAS constructs a suffix tree from a sliding window of recent trajectories.

**2. EfficientRollout (furiosa-ai, June 2026).** It compares the main types of drafters. It describes history-based methods, the group RANA would likely belong to, as ones that adapt non-parametric drafting by reusing rollouts from previous epochs as draft proposals, e.g., via prefix- or suffix-based matching.
- Their pros and cons: they are easy to deploy and require no parameterized drafter, but often yield short accepted drafts because past trajectories sparsely cover future rollouts. They also require a warm-up period to collect rollout history and may rely on acceptance-boosting heuristics such as reduced temperatures or lossy lenience settings.
- EfficientRollout itself reduces rollout and end-to-end latency by up to 19.6% and 12.7%, respectively, over an accelerated AR rollout baseline, while preserving final model quality.

**3. NVIDIA NeMo-RL speculative decoding (arXiv 2604.26779, Iso et al., April 2026).**
- The authors implement speculative decoding in NeMo-RL with a vLLM backend, supporting both synchronous and asynchronous pipelines and enabling speculation during RL rollouts.
- On agentic RL, they say the rollout bottleneck is growing there too, because long-horizon tasks require many repeated model calls across tool-use, retrieval, and web-interaction steps and further amplify the cost of every decoded token.
- They project that combining speculative decoding with asynchronous RL yields up to 2.5× end-to-end training speedup at 235B scale.
- On draft length: At 8B, k=3 is the sweet spot; k≥5 on RL-Think is actually slower than autoregressive decoding.


REMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks.

  ## Literature search: how similar parallel samples of one prompt are, and non-SD work that exploits it
  
  I checked all 47 arXiv IDs below against the arXiv API, and every title matches. 2506.17871 has been renamed "LLM Probability Concentration: How Alignment Shrinks the Generative Horizon". I did not write any files.
  
  ### Prior art you need to know first (SD work that drafts from siblings)
  - **Seer** (2511.14617, Nov 2025, Moonshot/Tsinghua). Its "Distributed Grouped Draft Server" keeps one compressed suffix tree per GRPO group, built from all sibling responses. This is your idea already shipped.
    - Table 2 (Qwen2-VL-72B, 20 groups), mean acceptance length for the linear drafter (multipath k=4 in brackets):
      - Own history only: 1.70 (1.85)
      - 1 sibling: 2.04
      - 5 siblings: 2.32
      - 15 siblings: 2.53 (2.85)
    - Grouped drafting accepts up to +119% more draft tokens late in the rollout.
    - Gains: +26–48% throughput from grouped SD, up to 2.04x end-to-end overall, and acceptance length +0.22 over a suffix tree without group context.
  - **Speculative Decoding for Multi-Sample Inference** (2503.05330, Mar 2025, preprint). It drafts from consensus across parallel paths: the last k tokens of a path are fuzzy-matched against the other paths, and candidates are merged in a DAG.
    - Accepted tokens beyond the bonus token, draft length 6, MATH: 1.89 vs 0.98 for EAGLE-2 (Qwen2.5-7B); 2.95 vs 1.48 (Llama3-8B).
    - Acceptance rises with the number of samples and peaks at intermediate temperature.
    - It reports no wall-clock speedup.
  - **Cross-epoch history drafters for RL rollouts:**
    - RhymeRL (2508.18588)
    - SPEC-RL (2509.23232)
    - DAS (2511.13841, MLSys'26 oral): one suffix tree per problem; per-problem trees beat a global tree; >50% rollout-time cut on math, ~25% on code.
    - BubbleSpec (2605.08862, May 2026): pre-generates drafts during long-tail idle time; 1.8x throughput.
  - **Counter-evidence: EfficientRollout** (2606.18967, NeurIPS'26). SPEC-RL-style history reuse covered only 4.4–50.2% of response tokens and gave +2–5% rollout time, i.e. no net gain, at large batch.
  
  ### Part 1: How similar are parallel samples?
  - **RhymeRL** (2508.18588, Aug 2025):
    - With a 3-token prefix lookup in last epoch's rollouts, 93% of tokens are matchable for math and 75% for code (14B, GRPO, 8 epochs).
    - Similarity rises over training. Live acceptance is 65–79%.
    - Most matched segments are 1–2 tokens long, but long segments carry most of the matched tokens.
    - It gives no within-group number.
  - **SPEC-RL** (2509.23232, Sep 2025):
    - Exact lossless prefix reuse from last epoch skips 24% of tokens overall and about 36% late in training (Qwen3-1.7B). These skip percentages are my calculations from its token-count tables.
    - Lenience e^0.5 skips 66–67%, at 2.31x average speedup.
    - Drafting from two epochs back is worse (1.44x vs 2.29x).
    - Its consecutive-epoch ROUGE-1 overlap is shown only as a figure.
  - **ReCo** (2607.26862, Jul 2026):
    - Uniqueness of the first 300 characters among 16 rollouts (Qwen2.5-Math-7B) falls from about 1.0 to 0.66 by GRPO step 580.
    - Token entropy falls from 0.605 to 0.041. Self-BLEU rises monotonically.
  - **S2L-PO** (2605.30789, May 2026): within-group Self-BLEU (AIME24, K=64) is 0.314 at 1.7B and 0.352 at 14B. Larger models are more homogeneous.
  - **Entropy Mechanism** (2505.22617, May 2025):
    - 73% of entropy loss happens in the first 200 of 2400 steps, and 94% in the first 800.
    - Fitted law R = −a·exp(H) + b.
    - It does not measure diversity directly.
  - **80/20 high-entropy tokens** (2506.01939, NeurIPS'25):
    - Qwen3-8B, T=1: 50.6% of CoT tokens have entropy below 0.01, and only 20% exceed 0.672.
    - Forks are therefore concentrated in a minority of tokens, mostly connectives like "wait" and "thus".
    - RLVR keeps 86.7% of the base model's high-entropy positions.
  - **Forking Paths** (2412.07961, Dec 2024, GPT-3.5): the share of examples with at least one outcome-changing fork token ranges from 0% (CoinFlip) to 27% (GSM8k), 43% (MMLU) and 63% (LastLetter). Forks can sit early, mid-sequence or near the end.
  - **Branching Factor** (2506.17871, TMLR'26):
    - Alignment cuts effective branching by 2–5x, and from about 12 to 1.2 at early positions.
    - Aligned models change by less than 10% from greedy to high temperature; base models change by up to 31%.
    - Distilled CoT models have even lower branching.
  - **Artificial Hivemind** (2510.22954, NeurIPS'25 D&B oral; open-ended prompts, 50 samples each):
    - At T=1, top-p 0.9, 79% of prompts have mean pairwise embedding similarity above 0.8.
    - At min-p with T=2, 61% still exceed 0.8.
    - Similarity between different models is 0.71–0.82.
  - **Path-Consistency** (2409.01281, Aug 2024): reuses majority-answer prefixes for later samples. Tokens drop 24–65%, latency up to 40.5%, with no accuracy loss. It gives no prefix-agreement statistics.
  - **UPFT / Prefix Self-Consistency** (2503.02875, Mar 2025): samples share their opening reasoning steps and errors appear late. It trains on 8–32-token prefixes.
  - **MoE fork redundancy** (2604.17182, Apr 2026; best-of-N code, T=0.7): 99.6% of differences within an assembly-equivalent group are comments or blank lines. Expert-routing Jaccard similarity is 0.649 at positions with the same token.
  - **Tree Training** (2511.00413): real Claude Code agent trees are 28–89% redundant shared prefix.
  
  **Gap:** I found no paper that directly reports sibling shared-prefix length or suffix-match length versus temperature for the same prompt. The nearest are Seer's Table 2 and the qualitative temperature curve in 2503.05330.
  
  ### Part 2: Non-SD work exploiting sibling or shared context
  
  **Shared-prefix attention (adjacent: exploits only the common prompt, not sibling outputs)**
  - Hydragen (2402.05099): up to 32x throughput.
  - FlashInfer cascade inference (blog, 2024-02-02; checked on flashinfer.ai, no arXiv ID): up to 31x over vLLM with a 32K shared prefix and batch ≥128.
  - FlashInfer (2501.01005, MLSys'25): 13–17% speedup for parallel generation.
  - ChunkAttention (2402.15220, ACL'24): 3.2–4.8x kernel speedup.
  - RelayAttention (2402.14808, ACL'24): up to 2.2x request rate.
  - Bifurcated attention (2403.08845): 2.1x at 16 samples and 6.2x at 32 samples.
  - DeFT (2404.00242, ICLR'25): 73–99% less KV IO, 2.23x end-to-end.
  - RadixAttention/SGLang (2312.07104): up to 6.4x throughput.
  
  **Tree-structured RL rollouts sharing prefixes (adjacent: they create shared prefixes by branching)**
  - TreePO (2508.17445): 22–43% fewer GPU hours.
  - TreeRL (2506.11902, ACL'25): branches at high-uncertainty steps.
  - ARPO (2507.19849): entropy-triggered branching after tool calls; half the tool budget.
  - AttnRL (2509.26628): branches at high-attention steps.
  - FR3E (2507.07017): rolls out from high-entropy points.
  - TreeRPO (2506.05183), Tree-GRPO (2509.21240, ICLR'26) and SPO (2505.23564, NeurIPS'25) take related approaches.
  - LEAF (2606.07610, EMNLP'26) is the closest of these: it builds a prefix tree after the fact from independently sampled responses.
  
  **Training and serving dedup (adjacent)**
  - Prefix Grouper (2506.05433): shared-prompt GRPO forward, cost approaching 1/G.
  - Tree Training (2511.00413): up to 6.2x.
  - ReasonCache (2507.21433): reuses KV blocks of similar reasoning steps across requests; +40–60% throughput.
  - Slim-SC (2509.13990, EMNLP'25 oral): prunes siblings whose thoughts reach similarity >0.98; up to 45% lower latency.
  - ST-BoN (2503.01422, NeurIPS'25 spotlight): truncates paths using early hidden-state consistency; 50% lower latency.
  
  **Parallel streams attending to each other's KV in flight (closest analogue to cross-sibling attention)**
  - Hogwild! Inference (2504.06261, NeurIPS'25):
    - Shared KV cache, RoPE re-stitching, no training.
    - QwQ-32B aggregate output: 20.1 tok/s (1 worker), 36.3 (2), 68.9 (4).
  - Group Think (2505.11107): interleaved KV with reserved position-ID slots; about N-fold fewer tokens per thinker early on.
  - LACE (2604.15529, Apr 2026): trained 2-D lattice cross-thread attention; more than 7 points over independent parallel search.
  - LaneRoPE (2605.27570, May 2026, ICLR'26 workshop): inter-sequence mask plus 2-D RoPE; maj@4 on AIME25 64.1 vs 50.1.
  - Multiverse (2506.09991), APR (2504.15466, COLM'25), ParaThinker (2509.04475) and Parallel-R1 (2509.07980): parallel branches, mostly without cross-branch visibility.
  
  **Bottom line:**
  - Siblings are highly copyable, and more so after RL: 75–93% of tokens are matchable across epochs, and acceptance rises with every added sibling reference.
  - Sibling-group drafting itself already exists in Seer (closest) and 2503.05330. Any novelty claim has to go beyond grouped suffix-tree or consensus drafting.
  - The open question is batch size. EfficientRollout found no net gain from history reuse at large batch, so a sibling drafter must be evaluated in that regime, not just in the long tail.
</agent-message>

content.content:
### TraSURE: Exploiting Cross-trajectory Recurrence to Accelerate Information-seeking RL Rollouts over Shared Corpora | qZ176Ev65f | 2026-09-10
Training agents with reinforcement learning (RL) to answer questions over shared corpora, such as enterprise knowledge bases, incurs substantial rollout cost. We identify cross-trajectory recurrence in this setting: trajectories for the same or different queries retrieve the same external items under different contexts, causing repeated prefill that group-based sampling further amplifies. However, this recurrence remains unexplored for rollout acceleration. We present TraSURE, which exploits this recurrence to accelerate RL rollouts over shared corpora. (1) For prefill, we use position-independent caching (PIC) to share recurring-item KV states across trajectories and avoid redundant prefills. (2) Building on this caching layer, we design demand-aware rollout scheduling to coordinate cache admission and retention using current and future item demand. (3) Beyond prefill, we use a next-outcome posterior to select historical continuations as drafts for posterior-guided speculative decoding. Across six models and four information-seeking workloads over shared corpora, TraSURE delivers up to $6.0\times$ speedup over standard rollouts, with all task scores within 1 pp of full-causal counterparts.

### GrowMTP: Can RL Grow Its Own Draft Head? | kol7DFYX4z | 2026-09-15
Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training drives the frontier capabilities of large language models, with its wall-clock dominated by autoregressive rollout generation.
Speculative decoding is an established remedy for this bottleneck, but existing draft heads must be pretrained or warmed up before RL, introducing substantial training cost outside the RL run to be accelerated.
We observe that RL training itself provides both conditions required for online draft-head training: its rollout distribution is far narrower than that of pretraining, and its verification step continuously produces supervision signals aligned with this distribution.
Building on these observations, we propose GrowMTP, which uses this supervision to train a draft head from scratch entirely within the RL loop, with all head updates detached from the policy backbone.
On Qwen3-4B (no draft head), MiMo-7B-SFT (weak head), and Qwen3.5-4B-Base (strong head), GrowMTP achieves rollout speedups of 2.13×, 1.93×, and 1.36×, and end-to-end speedups of 1.60×, 1.41×, and 1.20×, respectively.
GrowMTP therefore serves existing RL training frameworks as a modular component, particularly offering a from-scratch acceleration path for models without pretrained draft heads.
